RagShortTexts: The 1261 Treaty of Nymphaeum traded Galata commercial rights for Genoese naval war fleets.

Variants.Content: Concluded in March 1261 at Nymphaeum, the treaty bound Michael VIII Palaiologos of Nicaea to the Republic of Genoa. Genoa pledged up to fifty war galleys to help break the Latin hold on Constantinople and to check Venetian fleets. In return, Genoa received exclusive trading quarters in Galata, duty-free commerce, and commercial primacy across the Black Sea. The Genoese gained a foothold that lasted for generations, while the Byzantine emperor gained the sea power he needed to retake the capital. Each side accepted the bargain because neither could win a naval war alone.

Michael VIII traded commercial privileges across the Golden Horn to turn Genoese naval power against Venice, buying the fleet he needed to liberate Constantinople. Every trade quarter granted to Genoa was revenue the emperor gave up, which made the bargain a gamble on the outcome of the war.

Genoese galley crossbowmen work the rowing benches and the rails with iron discipline. When Nicaean signal fires flare across the Bosporus, Genoese ram-irons are ready to sink any Venetian cog that enters the straits. Keep your bolt case dry, count your quarrels before the signal, and never leave your station to chase a single enemy boat.

Greek caïque rowers watch red-cross banners multiply along the shoreline. Italian merchants drive hard bargains, but if Genoese steel drives the Latin usurpers into the Aegean, our families will feast under our true Emperor.
